Now, the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering is the ultimate goal of human endeavor (*atyantapuruṣārtha*). [This is the nature of the supreme goal of human endeavor. *KapSs* 1.1.
Its establishment is not [attained] through what is seen, because one observes its persistence even when [the worldly means] have ceased;
[this indicates that] the cessation of suffering is not possible through worldly means. (KapSs 1.2)
Its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) arises from the effort to counteract it, just like the daily counteracting of hunger;
[it is not achieved] through worldly means, because the cessation of suffering is impossible by such means due to their being entirely inadequate. (KapS 1.3)
Even if [liberation] were possible, it must be rejected by those skilled in the means of valid cognition because its existence is impossible;
for the cessation of suffering cannot be achieved through worldly means.
Furthermore, liberation is not [attained] through excellence, because scripture declares it to be the supreme excellence of all.
(The impossibility of the cessation of suffering through worldly means:
"And there is no distinction between the two" (KapSū 1.6).
[This implies that] even Vedic means are not the means for the cessation of suffering.

There can be no method for teaching the means to liberation for one who is bound by way of intrinsic nature; for bondage cannot logically be intrinsic, because that which is intrinsic is imperishable. (KapSs 1.7) [Bondage cannot be intrinsic because intrinsic nature is indestructible.]
Invalidity is characterized by non-performance [of the injunction].
(The inherent nature of bondage is untenable); nor is there an injunction for teaching what is impossible.

Even when instruction is given, there is no instruction [if bondage were natural]. (The impossibility of bondage being inherent): [Bondage cannot be natural] like a white cloth or like a seed. KapSs 1.10.

(The impossibility of bondage being inherent): Because of the emergence or non-emergence of power, there can be no teaching of the impossible. (The impossibility of bondage being inherent). It does not [arise] from connection with time, because that which is all-pervading and eternal is connected to everything; (thus, it is untenable for bondage to have time and place as its causes). Nor does it [arise] from connection with place for this same reason. (KapSs 1.12–1.13)
(Bandha cannot be caused by time or place:

It is not [caused] by state (*avasthā*), because that [state] is a property of the body. (KapS 1.14) (Bandha cannot be caused by a particular state: This is because [the soul] is distinct from such states.
"For this person is indeed unattached" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.15).

[The objection that] bondage must be caused by a specific state [of the self] is untenable; for it is not caused by action, since action is a property of something other [than the self], and because [if it were so] there would be an over-extension of the principle. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.16).

(The impossibility of bondage being caused by a specific state [of the self]: There would be no possibility of diverse experiences if [bondage] were a property of something other [than the mind]. KapSs 1.17:
(The impossibility of bondage being a property of the body of the mind.)
If it is argued that [bondage] arises from its connection with *prakṛti*, then even for that [*prakṛti*] there would be dependence on something else.
(It is untenable for bondage to have *prakṛti* as its cause.
For one whose very nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, there can be no connection with that [bondage], except through such a connection [with *prakṛti*]. (KapSs 1.18–1.19)
(The impossibility of bondage being caused by *prakṛti*):
Nor [can it be] from ignorance (*avidyā*), because bondage is impossible through that which is a non-entity. (The refutation of ignorance as the cause of bondage). *Kaṭhaśruti-bhāṣya* 1.20.
If it were a real entity, there would be a loss of the established tenet;
(this is the refutation of the view that bondage is caused by ignorance). Furthermore, there would be the consequence of a dualism between dissimilar categories.
(Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by ignorance:
If [bondage] were of two contradictory natures, [then...
(Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by ignorance), pū.
Because such categories are not perceived;
[this is] the refutation of the view that bondage has ignorance as its cause.
We do not maintain the doctrine of six categories like the Vaiśeṣikas and others.
(Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by ignorance):
Even if it were not restricted, there would be no inclusion of what is illogical;
otherwise, [the teaching] would be equivalent to that of children, madmen, and the like. (KapSs 1.26)
(Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by ignorance:
Nor is this [bondage] caused by the coloring [of the self] by various objects. (Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by the latent impressions of objects. *Kaṭhaśruti-sūtra* 1.27.

Nor is there a relationship of the coloring agent and the colored between the external and the internal due to spatial separation, as in the case of one residing in Srughna and another in Pāṭaliputra. (The refutation of the view that bondage is caused by the latent impressions of objects:
There is no fixed distinction [between the two] because the coloring obtained in one location does not apply to the other. KapSs 1.28–29.
(Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by the latent impressions of sense-objects:
If it is argued that [bondage occurs] by the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), [then the following applies].
(Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by the latent impressions of sense-objects), pū. [1.30]

Because two things cannot exist at the same time, there can be no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary [between them]. If it is argued that this is like the case of a son and his actions, [we reply:
No. (The refutation of the view that bondage is caused by the latent impressions of sense-objects).
If it is argued that it is like the case of a son and his actions, [we reply: No. KapSs 1.32.
(Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by the latent impressions of sense-objects):

There is no permanent, singular self there which is purified by such rites as the *garbhādhāna* (conception ceremony). (Refutation of the view that bondage is caused by the latent impressions of sense-objects). Sūtra 1.33. Sūtra.

Momentariness [is asserted] because stable effects are not established; [this is] the refutation of the doctrine of momentariness for all things, including bondage and so forth. However, this is further [rejected] because it is contradicted by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
(Refutation of the doctrine that all things, including bondage and so forth, are momentary):
This is also because it contradicts both scripture and logic.
(Refutation of the doctrine that all things, including bondage and so forth, are momentary).
And because the examples are unestablished:
[This is] the refutation of the doctrine of momentariness regarding all things, such as bondage and so forth.
There is no relationship of cause and effect between two things that arise simultaneously. (KapSs 1.37–1.38)
(Refutation of the doctrine that all things, such as bondage and so forth, are momentary: Because the subsequent cannot arise upon the disappearance of the preceding.
(Refutation of the doctrine that all things, such as bondage and so forth, are momentary.)

Because that [effect] is impossible in the absence of that [cause], and because both [cause and effect] would otherwise deviate from their respective natures, [the theory of momentariness] is untenable.
(The refutation of the doctrine of the momentariness of all things, such as bondage and so forth.
There is no necessary rule based on mere priority in existence. (KapSs 1.41)
(Refutation of the doctrine that all things, including bondage and so forth, are momentary:
It is not mere consciousness, because external objects are perceived.
(Refutation of the view that bondage and so forth have the nature of mere consciousness.)

Because of the absence of that [bondage and so forth] when that [consciousness] is absent, it is therefore empty; emptiness is the reality. (This is the refutation of the view that bondage and the rest are merely of the nature of consciousness. Emptiness is the ultimate principle.
An entity perishes, because destruction is a property of things.
(The refutation of the doctrine of universal emptiness), pū. 1.44.
The mere denial [of existence] belongs only to those who are not Buddhas;
(this is the refutation of the doctrine of universal emptiness). Since this [refutation] is equally secure for both sides, it is also [valid for the opponent]. (KapSs 1.46)
(Refutation of the Doctrine of Universal Emptiness) In both cases, there is a lack of human purpose.
(Refutation of the Doctrine of Universal Emptiness) KapSs 1.47.

Not from a particularity of motion; for that [particularity of motion] is impossible for one who is actionless. (The refutation of the view that a particularity of the self's motion is the cause of bondage. KapSs 1.48–49.
(Refutation of the view that a specific movement of the self is the cause of bondage:

Because it would possess form, like a jar or similar objects, it would result in the attainment of common properties [with material things], which constitutes an abandonment of one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*). (Refutation of the view that a specific movement of the self is the cause of bondage. *KapSs* 1.50.
The scripture concerning the movement [of the self] is also due to the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), like space.
(This refutes the notion that a specific movement of the self is caused by bondage.
Nor is it caused by karma, because [karma] is not its inherent property. 1.52.
(Refutation of karma as the cause of bondage) There would be the fallacy of over-extension if it were a property of something else. KapSs 1.53.
(Refutation of karma as the cause of bondage)
"And there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as [those describing Brahman as] devoid of qualities" (KapSs 1.54).
(The refutation of karma as the cause of bondage: "Even its connection [to the self] arises from non-discrimination; there is no equality [between the two]" (KapSs 1.55).
(The conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, caused by non-discrimination, alone is the cause of bondage);
its destruction results from a specific cause, like darkness. KapSs 1.56.
(Discrimination alone is the cause for the destruction of non-discrimination).

Through the non-discrimination of the primary cause (*pradhāna*), there is non-discrimination of other things; when that [non-discrimination of the primary cause] is abandoned, there is the abandonment [of all others].

(The fact that non-discrimination itself is the cause for the destruction of non-discrimination) is a mere verbal assertion and not the reality, because of the stability of the mind. (KapSs 1.57–1.58)

That bondage, though residing in the mind, is transferred to the *puruṣa* and is removable by the direct realization of one's own self (*svātmasākṣātkāra*), is not contradicted even by reasoning—just as the error of one confused about direction is removed by direct perception. (That bondage, though residing in the mind, is transferred to the *puruṣa* and is removable by the direct realization of one's own self. *Kaṭhaśruti-prakaraṇa-sūtra* 1.59. (That bondage, though residing in the mind, is transferred to the *puruṣa* and is removable by the direct realization of one's own self.)
The cognition of those things that are beyond the reach of the eye occurs through inference, just as fire is known through smoke and the like.
(The inferential nature of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*:
*Prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*). *KapSs* 1.60.
From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahān); from the Great One, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from the ego-sense, the five subtle elements (tanmātra).
The two types of sense organs arise from the subtle elements; together with the gross elements and the Puruṣa, this constitutes the group of twenty-five. (KapS 1.61:
The Establishment of the Twenty-five Principles)
From the gross [elements] comes the five subtle elements; (thus is the establishment of the twenty-five principles.
From both the external and internal [subtle elements] come those [gross elements], and from them comes the ego-principle. (KapSs 1.63)
(Proof of the Twenty-five Principles) Therefore, [this is] of the internal organ. (Proof of the Twenty-five Principles) *Kapila Sūtra* 1.64.
(Proof of the Twenty-five Principles)
From that [Prakṛti],
the establishment of the twenty-five principles [proceeds]:
because the Puruṣa exists for the sake of another who is composite.
(The Accomplishment of the Twenty-five Principles):
Since there is no root for the root, the root is rootless. (Prakṛti alone is the root of the entire world. *KapSs* 1.67.
Even in the tradition, the term "finality in one place" is merely a designation. (That *prakṛti* alone is the root of the entire world:
the *samāja* [is the union] of *prakṛti* and the two. (KapSs 1.68–69)
(Prakṛti alone is the root of the entire world:
there is no fixed rule because of the threefold nature of eligibility. (The reason for the non-universality of the contemplation of discrimination. KapSs 1.70.
The first effect, called the Great One (*mahat*), is that mind; its essential nature is the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*). The final [effect] is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
(The nature of the principle of egoity:
The subsequent principles [the tanmātras and so forth] have it as their effect.
(Even though the tanmātras and others are effects of egoity, their status as effects of primordial matter is established.)
The status of being the primary cause exists through that [intermediary] even in a successive sequence, as in the case of the atoms.
(Even though the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth are effects of the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), their status as effects of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is established.
When both [causes] exist in a prior state, if one is abandoned, the other is joined. *Kāpilasūtra* 1.74–75.
(That which determines that Prakṛti alone is the cause of all) is not a limited [cause], but the universal material cause;
(that which determines that Prakṛti alone is the cause of all).
And because of the scriptural statement regarding its arising from that [Prakṛti].
(The regulating factor for Prakṛti alone being the cause of all things is: the establishment of a real entity does not proceed from a non-entity. (KapSs 1.78)

The refutation of the emptiness of the world as the cause of the universe and the emptiness of the universe itself does not constitute [the proof of] their non-substantiality, because they are uncontradicted and produced by causes that are not defective. (KapSs 1.79)
(The refutation of the emptiness of the world's causality and the emptiness of the world itself:
If [the world] exists as a positive entity, its establishment occurs through its connection with that [emptiness].

In the absence [of that cause], since that [effect] would also be absent, how much less could its establishment occur? (This is the refutation of the void being the cause of the world and the world being the void. *Kapsūtra* 1.80.
Because it is not possible for karma to be the material cause [of the world]. (The refutation of karma as the material cause of the universe.
Nor is its establishment possible even through the revealed tradition (*anuśravika*).
Because it is not connected with non-recurrence as something to be accomplished, [worldly and Vedic actions] lack the status of being the goal of man.
(This is the refutation of worldly and Vedic actions as causes for the supreme goal of man.
In that regard, the scripture concerning non-recurrence pertains to the discernment of what has been attained. KapSs 1.83.
(Refutation of the claim that worldly and Vedic actions are causes for the supreme human goal:
Just as sprinkling with water [does not remove heat], there is no liberation from dullness from one suffering to another.
(Refutation of the claim that worldly and Vedic actions are causes for the supreme human goal.)
Whether in rites performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*) or those not so performed (*akāmya*), there is no difference in their status as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
[This concludes] the refutation of the view that worldly and Vedic actions are causes for the supreme human goal.
For one liberated from the seed [of karma], there is merely the destruction of bondage.
But there is no equality [between them].
(The refutation of worldly and Vedic actions as causes for the supreme human goal:
Valid cognition (*pramā*) is the determination of an object not previously perceived, whether by both [means] or by either one of the two.

That which is the most effective instrument for accomplishing that [cognition] is the threefold means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (The nature of valid cognition and the enumeration of the means of valid cognition.)

Since all [cognitions] are established when that [valid cognition] is established, there is no establishment of anything additional. (The nature of valid cognition and its dependence upon the means of knowledge. *KapSs* 1.88.
That cognition which, being connected [with an object], delineates its form is perception (*pratyakṣa*). (This is the definition of perception.
There is no fault [in this definition] because for yogis there is no perception of external objects.
(The definition of perception:
There is no fault [in this definition] because of the connection with the attainment of excellence regarding the hidden object. (The definition of perception) KapSs 1.91.
Because God is unestablished.
(The refutation of the existence of God as a subordinate factor: Since neither the liberated nor the unliberated exist [independently], He is not established. (KapSs 1.93)
(As a part of that, the existence of a Lord is refuted: In either case, [the opponent's position] is ineffective.
(As a part of that, the existence of a Lord is refuted. KapSs 1.94.
[This is] the praise of the liberated self, or [the praise] of one who has attained perfection through meditation. (As a subordinate part of that, there is the rejection of the existence of a Lord.
Through its proximity, [the self] exercises presiding control like a magnet. (KapSs 1.96)
(As a corollary, the existence of a Lord is refuted:
Even regarding specific effects, [the agency] belongs to the individual souls. (As a corollary, the existence of a Lord is refuted. *KapSū* 1.97.
Because the nature of the perfected one is that of a knower, there is the instruction on the meaning of the sentence.
(As a subordinate part of that, the existence of a Lord is refuted.
Because the internal organ is illumined by that [Self], its state of being a presiding controller is like that of iron [magnetized by a lodestone]. KapSs 1.98–99.
(The internal organ alone possesses the primary status of being the locus [of cognition]).
For one who perceives the probans, inferential knowledge is that which is based on the probandum. (This is the definition of inference. *KapS* 1.100.
Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person. (The definition of verbal testimony:
Its instruction is established for both [parties] through a means of valid cognition. 1.102.
(The result of the analysis of the nature of the means of valid cognition:

The establishment of both [the self and the external world] occurs through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). (The specific definition of inference in the form of *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*.)
Experience terminates in consciousness.
(The nature of valid cognition is free from defect.
Even for one who is not the agent, there is the enjoyment of the fruit, as in the case of food and drink. (KapSs 1.104–105)
(The resolution of the doubt regarding the difference in locus between agency and the enjoyment of the fruit:
Or, because that [agency] is established through non-discrimination, the agent is understood to experience the fruit.
(The resolution of the doubt regarding the difference in locus between agency and the enjoyment of the fruit.)
And neither [is it an object] when there is a true description of its nature;
for [objects] such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*) are conditions beyond the range of the senses.
An object may also be non-object due to excessive distance and so forth, depending on whether the sense organ is engaged in avoidance or acquisition. (KapSs 1.107–108)
(The conditions for the fact that primordial matter and the rest are not objects of the senses:
Its non-perception is due to its subtlety. (The conditions for the fact that primordial matter and the rest are not objects of the senses. *Kārikā on Sāṃkhya Sūtra* 1.109.
Because that [cause] is apprehended through the observation of its effect.
(The conditions for the fact that primordial matter and so forth are not objects of the senses:
If it is argued that this is unestablished due to the conflicting views of disputants, [we reply: KapSs 1.111.
(Definition of Satkāryavāda):
Even so, because one [of the two views] is established from the perspective of the other, there is no denial [of either]. (Definition of Satkāryavāda).
1.112. (Definition of Satkāryavāda). Conclusion.
And because threefold contradictions would ensue. (The Exposition of Satkāryavāda:
There is no production of the non-existent, like a human horn. *Kāpilasūtra* 1.113–114.
(Refutation of the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause:
Because of the restriction regarding the material cause.
(Refutation of the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause.)

Because everything would be impossible everywhere and at all times [if the effect were non-existent]; [this is] the refutation of the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavāda). Because that which is capable produces only that for which it has the capacity.
(Refutation of the theory that the effect is non-existent [asatkāryavāda]):
And because of the identity with the cause. KapSs 1.118.
(Refutation of the theory that the effect is non-existent.)
If it is argued that there is no connection with existence in the case of an existent thing (*sat*), [we reply:

the status of being an effect is established for what exists; moreover, the linguistic usages of "manifestation" and "non-manifestation" are not based on the actual production or non-production of the thing itself.
(The establishment of the effect as being existent): if destruction is the dissolution into the cause. (The nature of destruction).
Investigation by way of tradition is like [the sequence of] seed and sprout.
(In the view that [the effect] is manifested, the avoidance of infinite regress: As with origination, there is no fault. (KapSs 1.122–1.123)
(Resolution of the infinite regress regarding the theory of manifestation:
"That which has a cause, is non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, and indicative; (this is the nature of the effect). (KapSs 1.124)
Its establishment [as one] is due to directness, non-difference, or the commonality of qualities and so forth, or from the designation of the primary [cause].
(The nature of the effect) consists in the three qualities, insentience, and so on, which are present in both [the cause and the effect]. (KapSs 1.125–126)
(Regarding the similarity and dissimilarity between cause and effect:

The mutual dissimilarity of the *guṇas* is established by pleasure, pain, dejection, and so forth. (Regarding the similarity and dissimilarity between cause and effect. *KapSs* 1.127. (Regarding the similarity and dissimilarity between cause and effect.)
There is also a similarity of qualities with light and other such properties.
(Regarding the similarity and dissimilarity between cause and effect:
Because it is distinct from both, the state of being an effect belongs to the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest, just like a jar and so forth. (KapS 1.128–129)

(The proof that the Great One and so forth are effects) is from their finite dimension. (The proof that the Great One and so forth are effects) KapSs 1.130. (The proof that the Great One and so forth are effects)

Because of [the presence of] the concordance [of effects with their causes], and because of [the existence of] potency; thus is the establishment of the effect-nature of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest. (KapSs 1.131–132)
(The proof that the Great Principle [mahat] and the rest are effects: Upon its dissolution, it returns either to primordial nature (prakṛti) or to the spirit (puruṣa).
(The proof that the Great Principle and the rest are effects.)
If those two were different, [the effect] would be a mere nothingness. (The proof that the Great One and so forth are effects:
From the effect, one infers the cause because of their coexistence. KapSs 1.135.
(The method of inferring the cause from the effects:
The unmanifest [is inferred] from the mark consisting of the three qualities. (The dissimilarity of the primordial nature from its effects. *Kāpilasūtra* 1.136.
Because that [cause] is established through its effects, it cannot be denied. (The difference of the primordial nature from its effects:
Since there is no dispute regarding the general [existence of the cause], it does not require proof, unlike specific properties. (KapSs 1.137–138)
(Proof of the existence of the person:
The person is distinct from the body and so forth. (Proof of the existence of the person. *KapS* 1.139.
Because it exists for the sake of another through its composite nature;
[the proof of the existence of the Puruṣa] is from the reversal of the three guṇas and so forth. (KapSs 1.140–141)
(Proof of the existence of the Puruṣa:
"And because of the presiding [of the Puruṣa over the body]," KapSs 1.142.
(Proof of the existence of the Puruṣa.)
Because of the existence of the experiencer; [this is] the proof of the existence of the Puruṣa.
And because of the activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya).
(Proof of the existence of the Puruṣa: Light [is established] because the manifestation of an insentient thing is impossible.
(The Puruṣa’s nature as light: KSs 1.145.

Because it is devoid of qualities, consciousness is not a property [of anything else]. (This is the refutation of the relationship between property and its possessor for two things whose nature is luminosity.

The plurality of Puruṣas follows from the distinction of births and so forth. (This is the proof for the plurality of Puruṣas:
Even though there is only one [Puruṣa], it has various associations with different limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as space has [associations] with jars and other objects. (KapSs 1.149–1.150)
(The proof of the multiplicity of puruṣas: The limiting adjunct (upādhi) is differentiated, but not that which possesses it (tadvān). (The proof of the multiplicity of puruṣas. KapSs 1.151.
Thus, for that which revolves as a single unity, there is no superimposition of contradictory attributes.

There is no contradiction with the scriptures on non-duality, because [those passages] refer to the universal genus (*jāti*). (The justification for the doctrine of the unity of the Self. *KapSs* 1.154.
For one who has understood the cause of bondage, the vision is not of that [bondage] as having a real form;
(this is the justification for the doctrine of the oneness of the Self).
It is not through the vision of the blind that there is non-perception for those with sight.

(The justification for the doctrine of the identity of the self: Vāmadeva and others were liberated, not because of non-duality. (The justification for the doctrine of the identity of the self. *KapSs* 1.157.
Since it has been non-existent from beginningless time until now, it will likewise be so in the future.
(The proof of the doctrine of the oneness of the Self: Just as it is now, so it is everywhere; there is no absolute annihilation.

Witness-hood arises from direct connection;
[the self's] eternal oneness of form is its state of being eternally liberated. (KapSs 1.161–162)
(The souls are always of one and the same nature) and they are indifferent. (The souls are always of one and the same nature). KapSs 1.163.
(The souls are always of one and the same nature).

From proximity (*uparāga*), agency [is attributed]; from proximity to consciousness (*citsānnidhyāt*)—[this is] the cause for the appearance of agency in the *puruṣa* and the appearance of knowership in the intellect (*buddhi*), due to the inversion of the true nature of reality;
[it is] the effect of *pradhāna*.
[The purpose of the primary principle] is either for the sake of liberation from bondage or for its own sake;
[these are the constituent parts that serve as the cause for the creation of the world by Prakṛti], because it accomplishes that [liberation] for one who is dispassionate. (KapSs 2.1–2.2)
(Regarding the portions that serve as the primary cause for Prakṛti’s creation of the world:

Its realization does not result from mere hearing alone, because beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*) are powerful. (These are the portions of Prakṛti that serve as the primary cause for the creation of the world. KapSū 2.3. (Regarding the portions that serve as the primary cause for Prakṛti’s creation of the world.)
Or, like one with many servants, [the parts] exist individually.

(The parts that serve as the primary cause for the creation of the world from primordial nature) and, upon the reality of primordial nature, the establishment of the superimposition of the Puruṣa. KapSs 2.5.
(The refutation of the Puruṣa’s status as a creator:
Because that [creatorship] is established through its effects. (The refutation of the Puruṣa’s status as a creator. KapSs 2.6. (The refutation of the Puruṣa’s status as a creator.)
The restriction [of agency] follows from the designation of volition, like the removal of a thorn;
[this constitutes the refutation of the Puruṣa’s status as a creator].
Even if it were connected with something else, its accomplishment would not be direct, like the burning of iron by fire.
(The refutation of the Puruṣa’s status as creator:
The conjunction of passion and dispassion is creation. (The primary efficient cause regarding creation. KapSs 2.9.
The creation of the five elements proceeds by way of the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*).
(The creation of the Great Principle and so forth is for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.
Because creation exists for the sake of the Self, this undertaking of theirs is not for their own sake. (KapSs 2.10–11)
The creation of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest is for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa;
space and time [arise] from ether and the other elements. (The creation of space and time. *Kāpilasāṃkhyasūtra* 2.12.
Intellection (*buddhi*) is determination (*adhyavasāya*).
(The nature, effects, etc., of the Great Principle [the *mahattattva*]).
Its effects are virtue (*dharma*) and so forth. (KapSs 2.14).
(The nature, effects, etc., of the Great Principle [mahattattva]):
It is the opposite due to the coloring by the Great [Principle].
(The nature, effects, etc., of the Great Principle)
Self-conceit is the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-principle). (The nature, effects, etc., of the *ahaṅkāra-tattva*:
The eleven [faculties] and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are its effects. (KapSs 2.16–2.17)
(On the nature, effects, etc., of the principle of egoity:
From the *vaikṛta* egoity proceeds the group of eleven consisting of the *sāttvika* elements. (On the nature, effects, etc., of the principle of egoity. *KapSs* 2.18.
The eleven internal [organs] consist of the organs of action and the organs of cognition.
(This is the nature of the sense organs:
because of the scriptural statement that they are derived from *ahaṃkāra*, they are not composed of the material elements. 2.19–20.
(The nature of the sense organs:
The scriptural mention of them as abodes of deities does not apply to that which originates [them].
(The nature of the sense organs). KapSs 2.21.

Because of the scriptural teaching of their origination and because of the observation of their destruction, the sense organs are impermanent. (KapSs 2.22) For those who are deluded, the supersensuous sense organ resides in its physical substrate. (KapSs 2.23)
(The refutation of the view that the eyeballs themselves are the sense organs:
Even if there is a difference in their capacities, their distinctness is established; thus, they do not constitute a single entity.
(The rejection of the theory of a single sense organ.)
There is no contradiction with valid cognition regarding that which is perceived by the means of knowledge. (Refutation of the doctrine of a single sense-faculty:
And the mind is of a dual nature. *Kashyapa Śruti Sūtra* 2.25–26.
(The mind possesses the nature of both knowledge and action:
Its manifoldness, like that of various states, arises from the distinctions in the transformations of the *guṇas*. KapSs 2.27.
(The mind possesses the nature of both knowledge and action.)
From form up to the impurity of taste, these belong to both [the self and the senses].
(The objects of the senses are as follows: the capacity for seeing and so forth belongs to the self; the state of being instruments belongs to the senses. (KapSs 2.28–29)
(The sense organs being the effectors of the self): the specific characteristics of the three;
(the uncommon and common functions of the three internal organs). *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 2.30.
The common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa. (These are the specific and general functions of the three internal organs.
The function of the sense organs occurs both sequentially and non-sequentially. (KapSs 2.31–2.32)
(There is no rule regarding the sequential order of the functions of the senses:
The functions are fivefold, being either afflicted or unafflicted. (The five types of mental modifications. *Kaṭhaśruti-saṃhitā* 2.33.
Upon their cessation, [the Puruṣa] is tranquil, free from coloring, and established in its own nature;
at the very moment of the withdrawal of the mental modifications, the Puruṣa abides in its true form, like a gem with a flower [nearby]. (KapSs 2.34–2.35)
(Only at the time of the withdrawal of the functioning [of the guṇas] does the Puruṣa abide in its own essential nature.

Even the emergence of the instruments for the sake of the Puruṣa's purpose arises from the manifestation of the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa). (The limiting adjunct is the activity of the sense organs. KapSs 2.36.
Like a cow to her calf; (the limiting adjunct for the functioning of the senses). The instrument is of thirteen kinds due to its internal subdivisions.

Because they possess the quality of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) among the sense organs, like an axe. (The thirteenfold nature of the instruments). *KapSs* 2.39. (The thirteenfold nature of the instruments).
Between the two, the mind is primary, as in the world [the king is primary] among his circle of servants;
[this establishes the distinction between the subordinate and the principal among the instruments],
because of its non-deviation.
(Regarding the determination of the primary and secondary status among the instruments:
Likewise, because it is the substratum for all residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
(Regarding the determination of the primary and secondary status among the instruments.)
And because of memory and inference,
the distinction between the secondary and primary status among the instruments cannot exist by itself. (KapSs 2.43–2.44)

The relative state of being secondary or primary [among the instruments] depends on the specific action. KapSs 2.45.
(The determination of the subordinate and primary status among the instruments.)
Because it is acquired through that action, one exerts effort for its sake, as is seen in the world.

(On the distinction between the primary and secondary status among the instruments):
Because there is no distinction in the chapter on dispassion (*vairāgya*), the commencement of the specific [chapter] is for the sake of differentiation. *KapSū* 3.1.

From those five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), there is the gross creation which is the seed of transmigratory existence; from that [comes] the body. (KapS 3.2) (From the five subtle elements, there is the gross creation which is the seed of transmigratory existence.)
From that [seed], the cycle of existence arises. (From the five subtle elements, there is the gross creation which is the seed of the cycle of existence.
And due to non-discrimination, the manifestation of the non-specific [evolutes] proceeds.

(The cycle of transmigration ends in discriminative discernment.)
Now he is liberated from two [impurities]. (The limit of transmigratory existence is reached through discernment:
that which is born of mother and father is gross; for the most part, the other is not so.

The subtle body (*liṅga*) consists of seventeen components; it and its effects [are established].
The differentiation of individual manifestations arises from the particularity of karma.

It does not [act] independently, except through that [Self], like a shadow or like a painting.

And because of the scriptural statement that it consists of food (*annamaya*).

Transmigration for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), as the subtle bodies [serve] the king like cooks. (KapSs 3.16)
(The transmigratory nature of the subtle body as being for the sake of the person): The body is composed of the five elements.
(Differences of opinion regarding the essential nature of the gross body).

"Some say it consists of the four elements" (KapS 3.18). "Because consciousness is not a property of the elements, [the body] does not exist [as such]," [they argue]. "Others say it consists of a single element" (KapS 3.19).
(Caitanya is not a property of the elements):
Consciousness is not innate, because it is not observed in each [element] individually. (Caitanya is not a property of the elements).
And there would be an absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), death, and so forth.
[Furthermore,] there would be an absence of consciousness being a property of the elements.
If it is argued that it is like the power of intoxication—that which is not observed in each individual element arises when they are combined—then: *KapSs* 3.22.
(Consciousness is not a property of the elements.
Liberation arises from knowledge. (Bondage and liberation result from ignorance and the opposite of knowledge respectively. KapSū 3.23.

Bondage arises from the opposite [of knowledge]. (Bondage and liberation arise from the opposites of knowledge. Because they have fixed causes, there is neither a combination nor an option between them.
(The fact that the mere knowledge of reality is the cause of liberation:
Just as there is no liberation for a person from both the illusory and the non-illusory through dream and waking states respectively, [so it is with the world]. KapSs 3.26.
(The fact that the mere knowledge of reality is the cause of liberation.)
For the other [type of knowledge] as well, it is not absolute;
(there is an absence of the status of being a cause for liberation in knowledge consisting of meditation).
It is the same even in the case of what is mentally constructed.
(Upāsanā-attained knowledge is not the cause of liberation):
"Through the accumulation of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), for one who is purified, everything becomes as it was before. (The fruit of upāsanā). *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 3.29.
Meditation is the destruction of passion. (Regarding meditation’s status as the means for achieving liberation and knowledge: its accomplishment results from the cessation of mental fluctuations.
(The means for accomplishing dhyāna:
Its accomplishment comes through concentration (*dhāraṇā*), postures (*āsana*), and one's own practice. (The requisites for dhyāna, *KapSs* 3.32).
And their characteristics:
cessation [is achieved] through vomiting and suppression.
[These are] the means for accomplishing meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
And their characteristics are:
the posture is steady and comfortable; [these are] the means for meditation. (KapSs 3.34)
And their characteristics are as follows:
one's own duty (*svakarma*) is the performance of the duties prescribed for one's own stage of life (*āśrama*). [These are] the means for accomplishing meditation (*dhyānasādhanāni*). *KapS* 3.35.
And their characteristics [arise] from dispassion and practice. (For the primary qualified practitioner, there is no dependence on the five [restraints], beginning with *yama*. *KapSs* 3.36.
The varieties of error are five. (This is the classification of the errors that cause bondage.
However, incapacity is of twenty-eight kinds. *Kāpilasūtra* 3.37–3.38.

The varieties of contentment (*tuṣṭi*)—which are the incapacities that serve as causes for error—are ninefold. (This is the distinction between contentment and attainment, which produce incapacity of the intellect. *KapSs* 3.39.
Perfection is eightfold.
(The distinction between contentment and perfection, which bring about the incapacity of the intellect:
The intermediate subdivisions are as before.
(An explanation of the opposites, incapacity, contentment, and accomplishments: Thus it is for the other [eight].
(An explanation of the opposites, incapacity, contentment, and accomplishments.)
Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is ninefold due to the distinctions of the internal (*ādhyātmika*) and so forth.
(A brief explanation of error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment:
Attainment (*siddhi*) is eightfold through reasoning (*ūha*) and the rest. *Kāpilasāṃkhyasūtra* 3.43–44.
(A brief explanation of error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment: There is no attainment of one through the abandonment of another.
(Austerity and the like are not true attainments because they lack the nature of ultimate attainment.)
The divisions beginning with the divine [creation] (KapSs 3.46);
(the various divisions of creation beginning with the divine, as well as their limits) from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, that creation exists until the dawn of discrimination (KapSs 3.47).
(The divisions of creation such as that of the gods, etc., and their limits: Above is the realm expanded by *sattva*.
(The divisions of creation according to the differentiation of the *guṇas*. *KapSs* 3.48.
At the root, it is vast with *tamas*;
(due to the differentiation of the qualities, there are differentiations of creation);
in the middle, it is vast with *rajas*.
(The diversities of creation through the differentiation of qualities:
Due to the variety of karma, the activity of Pradhāna is like that of a slave born in the house; it is the cause of the diverse creations. (KapS 3.51)
Even there, one must abandon [the cycle] through successive higher unions;
until liberation, the state of being subject to creation is to be abandoned, for the suffering consisting of old age, death, and so forth is common to all. (KapSs 3.52–3.53)

(That the creations until liberation are to be abandoned: "One does not achieve the state of having fulfilled one's purpose through dissolution into the cause, any more than a diver who has risen [from the water]. (KapSs 3.54) [This indicates that even dissolution into *prakṛti* lacks the nature of absolute liberation.]
Even though it is not something produced, its connection [to the soul] occurs due to dependence [on primordial matter].
(The dissolution into primordial matter also lacks the nature of absolute liberation.
For he is the all-knowing and the maker of all. (KapS 3.55–3.56)

(The absence of the state of absolute liberation even for one merged in *prakṛti*): In this way, the proof of the Lord (*īśvara*) is established. (Only for one merged in *prakṛti* does there exist the status of a "Lord" among created beings. *KapSs* 3.57.
The primary creation is for the sake of another, because it itself is not an enjoyer. (The proof and purpose of creation having Pradhāna as its agent:
like a camel carrying saffron. (KapS 3.58–59)
(Justification and purpose of creation having Pradhāna as its agent) Even though it is insentient, the activity of Pradhāna is like that of milk. KapSū 3.60.
(Justification and purpose of creation having Pradhāna as its agent)
Or, like karma, [the effects] arise from time and so forth;
[this explains] the occurrence and purpose of creation whose primary agent is Pradhāna.
And activity proceeds from inherent nature due to the absence of intention, like that of a servant. (KapSs 3.61–3.62)
(Justification and purpose of creation by the Pradhāna as the agent):
Or rather, [creation proceeds] from the beginningless attraction of karma.
(Justification and purpose of creation by the Pradhāna as the agent).
Due to the realization of its isolation, the cessation of creation occurs for Pradhāna, as a cook ceases from cooking;
[this is] the cause for the cessation of creation.
[This occurs] because of the fault of mutual dependence.
(The cause for the cessation of creation:
Liberation is the indifference of one of the two [principles] toward the other. (The cause for the cessation of creation.)
Even when there is the coloring of another creation, one does not become dispassionate [toward it],
just as a serpent does not lose its nature when the reality of the rope has been realized.
(Because the cessation of one particular creation does not obstruct the commencement of another creation.)
And because of the connection with the cause that is karma. (KapSs 3.68) [This means:
due to the cessation of a particular creation, there is the absence of any obstruction to the commencement of another creation.
(KapSs 3.69) Even though [Prakṛti] is independent, non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is the cause for its assistance to Prakṛti.

(The establishment of the regulator for the activity and cessation of Prakṛti: Even for that which has begun its activity like a dancer, there is cessation because its purpose has been fulfilled. (The establishment of the regulator for the activity and cessation of Prakṛti.)
Even when defects are perceived, the primary matter does not approach [the Puruṣa], like a woman of good family; (this establishes the regulator of the activity and cessation of primordial nature).
Bondage and liberation for the Puruṣa do not occur absolutely except through non-discrimination. *Kārikā on the Sāṃkhya Kārikās* 3.71–72.
(Bondage and liberation do not pertain to the Self):
Because of the directness of *prakṛti* and because it possesses attachment, like a beast; (bondage and liberation do not pertain to the Self). *KapSs* 3.73.
Pradhāna binds itself with seven forms, like a silkworm binding itself with its cocoon, yet it liberates itself by means of a single form. (The causes of bondage and liberation:
The state of being a cause belongs to non-discrimination; there is no loss of what has been perceived. (KapS 3.74–75)
(The causes of bondage and liberation:

Through the practice of reality (*tattva*), by means of renunciation through "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), the perfection of discernment (*viveka*) is achieved. (The practice of reality alone is the cause of discernment. *KapSū* 3.76.
There is no fixed rule [regarding the duration of experience] because of the distinctions among those qualified [for practice].

(The fact that the practice of the principles alone is the cause of discriminative discernment) means that enjoyment may continue even through intermediate discernment by way of the persistence of what has been sublated. (KapSs 3.77–78)
(Only a specific degree of discernment is the means to liberation) and [he is] liberated while living. KapSs 3.79. (Only a specific degree of discernment is the means to liberation).
Its establishment [as a means] follows from the relationship between the teacher and the taught;
and there is also scriptural authority regarding this means for liberation while living.
(The means to liberation while living);
otherwise, it would be a blind tradition.
(The means to liberation while living). *Kaṭhaśruti-saṃhitā* 3.82. (The means to liberation while living).
Holding the body like the whirling of a potter's wheel— this is the means for liberation while living; its accomplishment arises from the remnants of past impressions.
(The means to liberation while living:

Through discernment (*viveka*), when all suffering has ceased, one has accomplished what was to be done; not through anything else, not through anything else. (In the Puruṣa, discernment alone is the cause of having accomplished what was to be done. *KapSs* 3.85.
The narrative is like that of the prince, because it provides instruction in reality; [this is] because instruction in reality is the cause of discernment. (KapS 4.1)
Even when instruction is given for another purpose, it is like [the case of] the Piśāca;
(the instruction of reality is the cause of discernment).
Repetition [is required] because of the repeated instruction. (KapSs 4.2–4.3)
(The instruction on reality is the cause of discernment),
because it is seen to be so for both [teacher and disciple], like a father and son. (In some cases, the knowledge of the body’s fragility arises from inference.)
Like a hawk, one experiences pleasure and pain through acquisition and loss;
like a snake shedding its skin, [one is freed from] the mental states that are the limbs for the perfection of knowledge.

(Regarding the factors for the perfection of knowledge, [the mind and phenomena are] like one whose hands have been severed. KapSs 4.7: (Regarding the factors for the perfection of knowledge, [the mind and phenomena are] like one whose hands have been severed.)
Contemplating that which is not a means leads to bondage, as in the case of Bharata. (The qualities of the mind are limbs for the perfection of knowledge.
There is conflict with many [impurities] in yoga, such as passion and the like, like a maiden [wearing] a bracelet (or a conch). 4.9. KapSs. 4.8–4.9.
(Regarding the factors for the accomplishment of knowledge, namely mind and phenomena:

by both of these it is likewise so. (Regarding the factors for the accomplishment of knowledge, namely mind and phenomena. KapSs 4.10. (Regarding the factors for the accomplishment of knowledge, namely mind and phenomena.)
Free from desire, one is happy like Piṅgalā;
[this is a quality of the mind that is a limb for the perfection of knowledge]. Even without exertion, one is happy in another's house like a snake. (KapSs 4.11–12)
(The factors for the accomplishment of knowledge:
the mental faculty and its object) Even when studying many scriptures and serving a teacher, one should extract the essence like a bee [from flowers].
(The necessity of grasping the essence) KapSs 4.13.
Like the arrow-maker, there is no loss of concentration for one whose mind is single-pointed.
(The necessity of one-pointedness.
By violating the established rule, there is futility, as in the world. KapSs_4.15.

(The necessity of not transgressing the rules prescribed by the scriptures, even when they are forgotten): "Even if they are forgotten, [the fault remains], like the female frog. (KapS 4.16) (The necessity of remembering the rules prescribed by the scriptures).
